Malik Mustapha wound up having quite a memorable Monday Night Football game against the Washington Commanders. Early in the game, the 49ers defensive back made a controversial hit on Stefon Diggs that could have been called a penalty for an illegal hit on the head and neck.

articles.headline: US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
keyFacts: The US Supreme Court agreed to hear a case concerning alleged racial discrimination in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools.
A parents' group claimed the admissions process discriminates against Asian-American students, while the school system argued the lottery is race-neutral.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and issue a ruling by June.
body: The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.

The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.
The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.
Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.
If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.
‘The Pandemic Plan’
The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.
It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.

The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.
Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.

“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
Previously thrown out

The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.
Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.
The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.

“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”
Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

articles.headline: In ruby-red Kansas, Trump contemplates the possibility of a Democratic win in the state
keyFacts: Donald Trump held a campaign rally in Kansas to support Republican Senator Roger Marshall.
Opinion polls show Marshall running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton for a seat Republicans held since 1932.
Voters will decide the contest during the midterm elections on November 3.
body: The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.

On Monday, amid raucous chants of “USA! USA!”, the president held his first campaign rally in Kansas for eight years. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in this ruby-red state since 1932, the year Herbert Hoover was president, Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag.

Since then Republicans in the state have built one of the longest winning streaks in Senate history, but such is the collapse in public esteem of the president that the midterms on 3 November could be the night that a blue wave engulfs the heart of Trump country.

“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”

The “guy” concerned was Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican senator facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Opinion polls show them running neck and neck. In the third quarter, Hamilton reportedly raised $11m while Marshall managed just $800,000.

Marshall, 66, is an obstetrician-gynaecologist and ex-congressman who has proved a staunch Trump ally, including by embracing his debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Hamilton, 62, founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the biggest United Methodist congregation in the country. He opposes Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president’s “erratic leadership”.

Despite Hamilton’s background as a pastor and former Republican, Marshall insisted on Monday that Hamilton was “too woke for Kansas”. Accompanied by Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode as he walked on stage, Marshall said: “This is a guy that participates in protests against police. He supports drag shows. He tells us to apologise for the colour of our skin. And in a state with more cattle than people, he tells you to stop eating beef.” The crowd jeered each time.

Trump, 80, is barnstorming the country in what some have called a “desperation tour” aimed at rescuing Republicans from the hole he has dug for them. Critics suggest he might actually be making life harder by nationalising races that candidates would prefer to keep focused on local issues.

By imposing himself in Kansas, at a rally that was disrupted by several protesters, Trump underlined the election as a referendum on his presidency, with the potential to cost Republicans control of both the Senate and House of Representatives just two years after they swept into power.

Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war: a gallon of diesel costs nearly $6. The president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home. On Monday Trump announced a new program to provide farmers with $8bn in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

The election will test whether the old playbooks that fuelled his presidential campaigns – hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies – can still work among an electorate weary of the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption.

Trump launched a tirade against Hamilton, dismissing him as a “radical left lunatic” and a “phoney who’s pretending to be a moderate”. Trump claimed the Democrat supports flooding Kansas with refugees who “go around killing people”, that he used church money to fund “transgender crap”, that he “openly mocks Jesus” and that he believes America is systemically racist.
“He wants you to repent for being born white,” Trump said.

The president also sought to weaponise the recent upheaval in France, pushing the baseless nativist claim that the violence is being led by immigrants. “We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”

Trump unleashed bitter attacks on three Muslim politicians: Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. When Tlaib’s name was mentioned, members of the crowd yelled: “Deport her!” Trump falsely claimed that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt. He mockingly warned that, should El-Sayed be elected and sit on the Senate intelligence committee, he would leak information to the enemy.

Supporters roared their approved, thrilled by what they saw as Trump’s transgressive daring. The president, who won Kansas by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, showed he can still draw a crowd in one of the most surprising battleground states in the country.

Earlier, in warm sunshine, a long line of people snaked through fields outside the 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas. There were sights that have become familiar over more than a decade: giant Trump flags, tables full of “Make America great again” caps, spangly “DJT” and “Trump the golden age” jackets, “Alligator Alcatraz” merchandise, “We are all Charlie Kirk now” sweaters and T-shirts that said “Stand for the flag, kneel for the cross”.
One woman wore a sweater that said: “0% liberal.” One man wore a T-shirt that declared: “I love Trump because he pisses off all the people I can’t stand.”

For these supporters, Trump rallies are galvanising and still the best way to get out the Republican vote. Cybersecurity worker Justin Nelsen, 44, said: “It fires us up, it gets us all excited for the cause and allows us to put out there what we want here as the state of Kansas. That’s why I’m here.”

Attendees were aware of the danger posed by Hamilton. Brittany Jones, a 33-year-old lawyer wearing a Stars and Stripes sweater, said: “If you know Adam Hamilton at all you know that he’s a problem and a chameleon and good at saying what he thinks people want to hear, even if he doesn’t believe it. He has shown himself to be not only a turncoat to things that matter to Christians, he has wholly given himself to the local agenda. Even though he claims to be a moderate, there’s nothing moderate about him.”

A Democratic victory here would represent a political earthquake, Jones acknowledged. “It’s seismic. It would be sad for most Kansans when they realise what happened, and some people just aren’t thinking through the consequences, but he has a built-in audience of people who are highly motivated.”

Jones, who had her friend’s three-month-old baby, Hannah, tucked under one arm, said she mostly welcomed Trump’s second term. “Overall I care about the social issues and he’s done a lot to protect girls’ sports, he’s done a lot to protect kids from being put through harmful gender transition procedures. Those things matter to me, they matter to the future of girls all across Kansas and America, and so I’m excited about those things.”
Construction worker Thad Snider, 42, who attended wearing a red “Make America Great Again” T-shirt alongside his mother, said he was not overly worried about the Senate seat falling to the Democrats.

“I don’t think Adam’s as strong a candidate as what the media is trying to sell him as,” he said, pointing to Hamilton’s past political donations to Democrats including Hillary Clinton. “I don’t think it’s going to happen but, if it did happen, it would be very shocking.”

Snider argues that voters faced a stark choice between political parties, describing the Republicans as the “least bad” option because “at least they’re not socialists or communists”. He added that he disagreed with foreign wars and wished Trump had done more on election integrity, but remained loyal to the president. “Any time you turn around a battleship, it takes time.”

That sentiment was echoed by Darrell Claphan, 72, a retired sales worker, who said of Trump: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”
Claphan dismissed opinion polls showing a close race, stating: “Polls have been wrong ever since I’ve been alive.”
Asked how he would react to a Democratic Senate victory in Kansas, Claphan said: “I’d be shocked. But I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

articles.headline: Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
keyFacts: Baseus announced the PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera, which features a motorized spotlight that tracks moving targets.
The camera is available now on Amazon in the US for $269.99 and will launch in Europe on October 15th for €269.99.
The device includes AI-powered motion alerts, dual 3K cameras, local storage on a 512GB memory card, and a rechargeable battery lasting up to 150 days.
body: Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.
Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
The Baseus U2 Pro can deter intruders instead of just capturing them on camera.

The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.

Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.

Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

articles.headline: Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years
keyFacts: Christiane Amanpour announced on Monday that she is leaving CNN after 43 years at the network.
Her departure follows Paramount Skydance's takeover of CNN's parent company, which prompted concerns regarding newsroom independence.
Amanpour stated her daily show will end this year, followed by a weekly program airing through June.
body: Veteran journalist Christiane Amanpour on Monday said she was leaving her role at CNN after 43 years at the network.
"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN," Amanpour, 68, said in a statement.

"This daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year. But CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition where we continue doing Amanpour once a week through to June," she said in a video message posted on social media.
Amanpour, who became famous for her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones, did not give a reason for her departure.
That said, her move to resign comes weeks after CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), was formally taken over by Paramount Skydance.
After a yearlong process, Paramount closed its merger with WBD on October 6, uniting two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN — under one roof.
The merger has drawn concerns over the independence of the newsroom at CNN as the merged company's owners, the Ellison family, are close allies of US President Donald Trump.

"You know I've always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you as long as I am here and beyond. That's especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field," she said, without directly referring to the deal.
What to know about Amanpour's career

Amanpour, who was born in London to an Iranian father and British mother, joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant. In the next few years, she went on to cover major wars in the 1990s, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War.
Amanpour has interviewed many world's leaders, reported from conflict sites and interviewed newsmakers from hotspots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda and the Balkans.

She said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."
In a memo, CNN Chief Executive Mark Thompson praised Amanpur for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally," Thompson said.

articles.headline: Brock Purdy becomes highest-rated passer in NFL history as 49ers stay perfect
keyFacts: Quarterback Brock Purdy became the highest-rated passer in NFL history after passing the 1,500-attempt threshold during the game.
The San Francisco 49ers defeated the Washington Commanders 23-17 to achieve their sixth straight win to open the season.
Jayden Daniels threw two second-half touchdown passes to cut the deficit, but the 49ers secured two late defensive stops to preserve the win.
body: Brock Purdy threw a touchdown pass, Christian McCaffrey ran for two scores and the San Francisco 49ers held on to beat the Washington Commanders 23-17 on Monday night for their sixth straight win to open the season.
The Niners followed up an emotional win last week at division rival Seattle by building a 20-point lead and holding off the Commanders (1-4-1) with two late defensive stops.
“[The defense] did it for us all game, I’m proud of those guys ... our defense balled,” Purdy said after the game.

Jayden Daniels threw two touchdown passes in the second half to cut that 20-point deficit to 23-17, but Malik Mustapha broke up a fourth-down pass to Treylon Burks near the goalline with 1:54 to play to preserve the lead.

Washington got the ball back at its 46 with 52 seconds remaining and moved down to the 28 before Daniels was called for intentional grounding, giving the Commanders one last play from the 40. Daniels was then sacked by Keion White and Ogbo Okoronkwo before he could throw up a desperation pass.
The Niners extended their best start of a season since winning their first eight games in 2019 on the way to a Super Bowl appearance.

Purdy started the game fast with a 24-yard strike to Mike Evans, who later left the game with an achilles injury, on the third play of the game and an 11-yard touchdown to George Kittle to finish that drive. Purdy went 21 for 29 for 264 yards and officially became the highest-rated quarterback in NFL history as he passed the 1,500-attempt threshold to qualify. His 105.6 rating is ahead of Lamar Jackson’s 102.7.
The Commanders were unable to bounce back from last week’s tie against the New York Giants, when they mismanaged the clock in overtime to cost them a chance at a game-winning field goal.
The game was one-sided early with the 49ers scoring touchdowns on the first two drives on Purdy’s pass to Kittle and a one-yard run by McCaffrey.
San Francisco expanded the lead to 20-3 late in the half on McCaffrey’s second touchdown run as the Niners gained as many first downs (17) in the first half as the Commanders ran plays.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy says it's Putin who wants an endless war, not him
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy stated Monday that Russian missile and drone strikes hit energy and residential infrastructure without partner warning.
President Trump accused Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war, while the U.S. eased sanctions on Russia.
Zelenskyy asserted that Russian President Putin wants an endless war and criticized U.S. officials over alleged supply and intelligence limits.
body: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Monday that his country had been subjected to another night of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners."

Zelenskyy has accused the U.S. of limiting intelligence, and possibly other assistance to Ukraine amid renewed tension with President Trump, who accused the Ukrainian leader over the weekend of not wanting to end the war. Mr. Trump has significantly softened the U.S. government's policy toward Russia, easing sanctions to allow Russian energy sales in a bid to ease U.S. gas prices.
Zelenskyy says the moves risk emboldening Moscow and enabling it to continue and intensify its four-and-a-half-year, .
The target of the most recent strikes was energy and other infrastructure, Zelenskyy said, adding that a medical clinic, school, metro station and "ordinary residential buildings" were also hit.

Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite technology, to intercept Russian drones. The network is crucial to Ukrainian forces as it enables them to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones and other weapons.
The Trump administration has denied making any changes to the intelligence it shares with Ukraine, or deliberately slowing down Starshield data.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

Asked Saturday if the U.S. government was responsible for the change in Starlink service in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate … we have nothing to do with that."

"The United States — nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before," he said, without elaborating on what he meant by "it sort of happened."

Denys Sienik, Ukraine's chargé d'affaires and current top diplomat in the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or Musk's SpaceX to inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."

"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X, adding that there had also been "delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War."
He did not expound on his assertion that the Pentagon was delaying shipments of supplies.

The Ukrainian leader issued the statement amid an increasingly terse exchange of accusations with Mr. Trump who, over the weekend, accused Zelenskyy of not wanting the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion to end.
In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump argued.

The U.S. president has over the last month walked back sanctions on Russia — that had support from a majority of Republicans and Democrats — that were intended to increase financial pressure on Moscow over its assault on Ukraine.
"Ukraine never wanted this war," Zelenskyy said in another statement shared Monday on social media. "We took positively literally EVERY attempt of partners to end this war with dignity."

Just over a week ago Mr. Trump declared in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," which would mean a halt to attacks on the other country's energy infrastructure. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to any such deal, and within hours Ukrainian authorities reported new Russian attacks on refineries.
Zelenskyy said "again and again Russia's answers" to efforts at diplomacy were new attacks.

"Putin does not want the end of this war, or even any de-escalation steps," he said, adding: "It is very important to call things by their names. Call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine protect lives. When the supply of missiles to Ukrainian air defense is blocked, and Russia receives a weakening or postponement of sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality from partners. In reality, the war continues, and continues only because of Russian strikes — the Russian desire to prolong this war."
The Kremlin, meanwhile, has attempted to frame Russia as a willing partner in peace efforts.

Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Moscow values U.S. mediation efforts, but that reaching agreements without the participation of representatives from Kyiv is impossible. There have been direct talks, mediated by the U.S., between Ukraine and Russia, but so far the meetings have yielded little more than prisoner swaps, not ceasefires.

The Wall Street Journal first reported Sunday evening that Putin had proposed a meeting between U.S., Chinese and Russian officials to discuss solutions to the Ukraine war, but without a seat for Ukraine at the negotiating table. The newspaper said he proposed the idea for a summit during a call with Mr. Trump on Oct. 9.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Monday in a post on X that "a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."

articles.headline: North Korea releases photos of Kim Jong Un at clothing expo after viral death rumors

body: North Korean state media published photos of Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un on Monday after viral rumors of his death stormed social media over the weekend.

The newly released images show Kim at a clothing and shoe expo with his daughter. He appeared well and fit, seemingly disputing unverified claims that he had fallen into a coma and died of a brain hemorrhage. According to these rumors, he had been taken to a hospital in Beijing.
NEW: Kim Jong Un on Monday "looked round the venue of the garment and footwear exhibition of the field of light industry," DPRK state media said.

None of the claims, spread by Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie on X, have been confirmed.

At first, Xie claimed Kim died and that China dispatched 9,000 troops to Pyongyang, North Korea, over fears of a succession crisis. Then he alleged that the dictator’s body was secretly transported to North Korea.
In his latest post , Xie said the rumors of Kim’s death are “likely true” because Kim hadn’t made a public appearance before the photos were released.
It is unclear whether the photos of Kim are authentic or when they were taken.
The rumors raised questions about whether Kim’s sister or daughter would succeed him.
TRUMP SAYS HE MAY MEET WITH KIM JONG UN DURING ASIA TRIP

Xie initially claimed that the North Korean supreme leader’s daughter, Kim Ju Ae, was handed the regime before saying his sister, Kim Yo Jong, took control. The sister is the director of the General Affairs Department of the Workers’ Party of Korea, while the daughter is viewed as Kim’s likely successor by South Korea’s intelligence agency.
Coincidentally, the rumors of Kim’s death arrived just before the Oct. 23 video game release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , in which North Korea launches a full-scale invasion of South Korea.

articles.headline: Trump says voters should ‘look at France’ to see ‘what’s at stake’ in midterm elections
keyFacts: At a Kansas rally, Donald Trump cited riots in France as an example of what is at stake in the midterm elections.
Authorities reported at least 2,400 arrests and 3,000 damaged businesses during protests in France over school conditions and inflation.
Trump visited Kansas ahead of the November midterm elections to campaign for Senator Roger Marshall and gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson.
body: President Trump framed the upcoming midterm elections as a battle for “Western civilization” on Monday, pointing to a wave of violent riots in France.
“If you want to see what’s at stake in this election, just look at France,” Trump said at a rally in Wichita, Kansas.
The president described France as “a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity.”
“And they hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself,” Trump added.
At least 2,400 arrests were made over the weekend as violence and looting broke out across the country, including in the capital city of Paris.
The student-led protests began last month over school conditions and have broadened to focus on the cost of living and inflation.
Authorities estimate that at least 3,000 businesses have been damaged or ransacked in several cities.

“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember, that is what the radical Democrats want to do to America,” Trump charged. “They expect to do it. They’re not going to come close.”
The president declared that “the Democrat agenda is a plan to extinguish Western civilization.”

“They want to open the borders … They want to shut down our power plants. They want to set loose the criminals, turn your children transgender, confiscate your money and raise up the Palestinian flag right in the middle of your wonderful state and, at the same time, they’re willing to defile our great and very beautiful American flag,” Trump continued, reiterating, “We’re not going to let that happen.”
Trump blamed “third-world migrants” and “globalist left-wing politicians” for the turmoil in France.

“They’ve surrendered their country to vandals,” the president said of French leaders, describing the protesters as migrants who “refuse to assimilate” and “only want to enter the welfare state paid for by hardworking citizens of France.”
“This is what’s happening to France. They want it to happen to our country.”
Trump made the trek to Kansas as part of his whirlwind red-state tour ahead of the November midterms.
At the rally, Trump boosted incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) – calling him “one of the best” in the Senate – and GOP gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson.
The president also expressed his condolences for the victims of a “horrific car crash” in Wichita over the weekend that injured 10 people and killed two, including a 6-year-old boy.
“We grieve for the beautiful lives that were lost. And pray for those who were tragically injured,” Trump said. “What a horrible event.”
The 34-year-old driver who smashed her vehicle into a crowd at the Stryker Sports Complex Saturday afternoon has been released without charges.

“We want to get to the bottom of what happened,” Trump said of the tragedy. “That was a terrible thing. And we’re going to give, and you have great law enforcement, but we’re going to give them whatever help they need.

articles.headline: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu for reelection, diverging from Trump

Vance stated that he only endorses American candidates and is focused on the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump backed Netanyahu for reelection on Sunday, calling the prime minister a critical ally against Iran.
body: Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection on Monday, a day after President Donald Trump backed the Israeli leader’s bid.
When journalist Mark Halperin posed the question, Vance laughed before giving a brief response .

“The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history,” he said. “I endorse American candidates, and that’s what I’m focused on, is the midterms. So I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections.”
Pressed again on the matter, the vice president said he is neither in favor of nor opposed to an endorsement of Netanyahu but doesn’t want to get involved in Israeli politics.
Earlier this year, Trump and Vance endorsed former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban for reelection. Their support didn’t do much, as Orban lost the election to Peter Magyar.
Vance’s decision not to weigh in on Israel’s Oct. 27 legislative election is notable, considering Trump has been a strong ally of Netanyahu for some time.
TRUMP BACKS NETANYAHU FOR REELECTION, SAYS ISRAELI PM CRITICAL ALLY AGAINST IRAN
Trump voiced his support for Netanyahu in a Truth Social post on Sunday, telling Israelis to vote for the embattled prime minister because he is a great foe of Iran .

“It would have been only a question of time until Iran would have put that ominous phrase into effect, but they have been systematically destroyed, both Militarily and Financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job,” Trump wrote. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so.”

articles.headline: ICANN testing tech to let law enforcement access non-public WHOIS info
keyFacts: ICANN is testing authentication technology to let law enforcement agencies request non-public WHOIS domain data during urgent threats.
The system uses Security Assertion Markup Language to allow verified personnel at agencies like the FBI and Interpol to file requests through the Registration Data Request Service.
Domain registrars will have 24 to 72 hours to review and potentially deny requests that do not meet the set urgency threshold.
body: ICANN has started testing authentication schemes that will allow law enforcement agencies to make urgent requests for non-public WHOIS information – when needed to address threats to life, critical infrastructure, or child exploitation.

Domain registrars collect information about their customers and in the past that data was publicly available in WHOIS records. Some domain registrars offer services that substitute their own contact details, to preserve customer privacy. In recent years, laws like GDPR mean registrars are sometimes required to hide WHOIS data.

That’s fair enough but makes it hard for law enforcement to contact a domain holder if their resources are being misused – intentionally or otherwise – for purposes such as hosting malware, acting as command-and-control infrastructure for malware, or facilitating phishing.

ICANN’s definition for the kind of behaviour it thinks justifies urgent requests for WHOIS info is “imminent threat to life, of serious bodily injury, to critical infrastructure, or of child exploitation.”

The org has convened an Input Group on Law Enforcement Agency Authentication Mechanisms to consider the issue, and that group yesterday explained its progress during ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali, Indonesia.
At this point, readers may have concerns that this proposal could allow law enforcement authorities to make inappropriate requests for WHOIS information.
Several factors may ease such concerns.
One is that representatives of domain registrars Namecheap and Verisign spoke during the session about the proposal, and both were supportive.

Another is that the Input Group’s work is largely technical. Once it devises a mechanism to allow requests, other groups within ICANN dedicated to policy will work out acceptable use and related issues.

This is the way internet governance gets done! Specialists work on their own bits of a problem and then collaborate to create a robust system that works at a technical level, is practical, and enforceable in multiple jurisdictions.
How they’ll do it

At this point, ICANN’s preferred approach is to use Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) so that authenticated users at law enforcement agencies can log into the governance org’s Registration Data Request Service (RDRS) and file requests to access non-public WHOIS info. ICANN is already testing this approach with the FBI and Interpol but is open to other authentication mechanisms to allow other agencies access RDRS. The Input Group’s aim is to publish a spec those agencies can conform to.

ICANN will pass requests filed in RDRS to whichever registrar sold the domain. The registrar will have 24 hours to consider the request – or up to 72 hours for complex queries. Registrars will also be able to deny requests if they feel the query does not meet the urgency threshold.
Register readers might worry that a colossal agency like the FBI could flood RDRS with requests from thousands of individual agents, swamping domain registries.

ICANN’s plan is to avoid that by requiring law enforcement agencies to nominate certain personnel who are permitted to make requests, and to enforce that permission using a token shared during SAML handshakes. The content of that token is the kind of policy question that the Input Group expects others at ICANN to finalize later.

Another issue under consideration is how to protect the identity of law enforcement workers who make RDRS requests, as ICANN feels they could become targets of harassment (or worse) if their requests to see WHOIS data include email addresses. ®

body: Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers took aim at Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed during a town hall with Fox News host Sean Hannity on Monday, warning voters that his rival's policies would hurt the state.
Rogers accused El-Sayed of having a "pattern of deception" and called him a "manufactured candidate," claiming the Democrat has misrepresented his political positions.

articles.headline: Walmart’s Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India
keyFacts: Walmart-owned Flipkart is internally testing a food-delivery service in Bengaluru and expanding trials to over 8,000 employees.
Flipkart plans to publicly launch its food-delivery service by the end of October and expand to five or six cities by year-end, according to Sagar Daryani.
Flipkart enters a market dominated by Zomato and Swiggy, offering restaurants a lower base commission of about 10%.
body: Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in.

The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch.

The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms, as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly.
Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered.

As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions.

Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing, a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay.

“Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.”
Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms.

Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru, but it shut the service down two years later. Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato.

Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.
“Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch.

Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy.

Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order.

Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them.

Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. The company has told restaurants that it expects to launch its food-delivery service publicly by the end of October and to expand to five or six cities by the end of this year, Daryani told TechCrunch.

The food-delivery push also comes as Flipkart’s long-awaited stock-market listing remains uncertain. Chief Executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above) recently declined to give a timetable for an IPO, even as the company continues to expand into businesses that could bring customers back to its app more frequently.

Flipkart’s expansion comes as competition in India’s e-commerce market intensifies. Quick-commerce platforms that started by delivering groceries in minutes now sell even the latest iPhones and other discretionary purchases, putting them in more direct competition with Flipkart and Amazon.
Flipkart did not respond to a request for comments.

articles.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Pop-Up: The DMZ Has Never Been This Much Fun
keyFacts: Sydney recently hosted a limited-time, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 pop-up experience featuring virtual and physical challenges based on a Korean demilitarised zone.
Attendees chose to represent either North or South Korea, completing passport tasks that included campaign gameplay, stealth challenges, and finding propaganda documents.
IGN reported that Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ Early Access starts on October 21 for preorders, with the full game launching on October 23.
body: Having just returned to Oz from a review trip at Infinity Ward, I was in a pretty good position to judge how authentic (and fun) a Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Pop-Up Experience could be. As luck would have it, Sydney recently hosted just such a shenanigan for press, content creators, lucky Xbox Fan Fest attendees and there were some limited slots open to the public via registrations. I infiltrated it fully.

Let me bust out my Tac-map and give you a sitrep on how the organisers decided to… well, run DMZ (as in a recreation of a real Korean demilitarised zone). The result was a limited-time, MW4-themed mini-extravaganza built around a series of virtual and physical challenges. In next to no time, my objectives list was overflowing with around a dozen POIs to visit across the Carriageworks event space.
Think interactive games, hands-on MW4 Campaign gameplay, photo opps and prizes for the exceptionally skilled.

To be honest, I wasn’t sure if I would be among the exceptionally skilled. Working in my favour: I was one of only a handful of folks who’d already finished MW4 (and on its unlockable Realism difficulty, no less). Working against that massive headstart: 15 hours of jetlag and severe sleep deprivation.
It was a 50/50, comrades. I’d blitz this event or pass out midway.

When about sixty of us were marched into the event, I was mighty impressed with the dank, smoke-machine-assisted scene that greeted me. The organisers had nailed the DMZ duality aesthetic of two vastly different Koreas fighting over the one peninsula. Entry required picking a side, North or South, and a razor wire fence bisected the space as a roving spotlight made sure nobody defected.

Better yet, upon selecting which Korea to go with, a decision facilitated by uniform-and attitude-appropriate personnel, I was issued a passport with tasks to complete. Call me a communist, but I chose the NK and, at the risk of being hunted down as a traitor later, I can detail my time spent in the North.
I’ll let my issued Military Passport give you the gist of what was expected of me:
“Congratulations. You have been selected to serve the Northern Command, an honour granted to very few and refused by NONE.
Across this territory you will find operations. All participation, success or failure, will be stamped in this permit. Every stamp is yours to keep. Every victory, however, belongs to the North.”

Being proactive, I elbowed through a small sea of comrades to skip past the minigames, ascend centre stage and smash out a COD MW4 Campaign mission. Easy stamp, right there, folks. Side bonus: I even got some of my exploits replayed up on a screen the size of Kim Jong Il’s home cinema setup (he was quite the movie buff).
With early dominance secured, not only for myself, but for the glorious North entire, I descended back down into the other activities.

Honestly, there were some pretty nifty things to do. Operation Crossfire had me donning some NVGs and disappearing into a pitch-black shipping container to “acquire a target”. Once the traitor had been found and dispensed with, I moseyed over to Contraband Sweep and located anti-government items under threat of a time limit.
Glowing from my victory, I went and got a State Portrait, where I was informed that the North does not photograph happiness, only my resolve. I adjusted my smile accordingly.

The fun continued with me snooping around the space to find and secure Daily Truth propaganda documents. I also hunted down and confronted a (not-so) Covert Operative who was skulking about with a smug, democratic way about them that disgusted me to my very core. Upon confronting this Task Force 141 agitator, I seized their permit and uttered the codeword hidden within. His shame at discovery was palpable. The glorious North earned another stamp.

Before making my way to the Armoury to secure my booty, I infiltrated the South side to witness how life was for Capitalist hooligans. On account of the bile repeatedly rising up my throat while in their presence, I didn’t see everything these bourgeois delinquents got up to. I did, however, notice that they were earning their own stamps for defusing bombs with aid provided by troops in full kit.

What overwhelmingly was worth it, however, was attending this wonderful, MW4-themed side diversion. In case you haven’t read our review-in-progress yet, the general consensus (which includes me) is that the Campaign is quite a return to form for Infinity Ward.
Or, to put that more succinctly, the solo pillar of this sequel, and the pop-up event inspired by it, are stamp-worthy. And you can put that in your permit with confidence, comrade.

articles.headline: 3 Video Games Where Your Choices Actually Make a Difference
keyFacts: Polygon published a list highlighting three video games that use branching narratives in unexpected ways.
The games featured are Zero Parades: For Dead Spies, Slay the Princess, and The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy.
Each game uses player choices differently, ranging from shaping character stats and psychological states to drastically altering entire storylines and endings.
body: This year's open-world RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker and its myriad choices got me thinking: What does it really mean for your choices to matter in a video game? Typically, we think it's a good use of branching narratives when you have a properly big, dramatic effect on how things play out or when you have hundreds of endings. Just look at how so much attention on Baldur's Gate 3 focused on its endings or, years before, how everyone tended to ignore the smaller ways the Mass Effect trilogy changed across three games in favor of looking at the restrictive outcomes in Mass Effect 3.

Large-scale narrative branches are engaging for a reason. They're satisfying, and they make you feel a sense of influence over events and characters you care about. Like with video game romance, however, they have become somewhat stale and predictable in form. So for this list, I decided to look at three games that use branching narratives in bolder and unexpected ways.
3 Zero Parades: For Dead Spies
Release date: May 1, 2026
Where to play: Windows PC (with Nintendo Switch 2 and PlayStation 5 versions planned for November 2026)

Zero Parades: For Dead Spies is the rare piece of interactive media where your choices matter not just for how they influence the story, but for how they shape your actions, too. Hershel, the protagonist of the piece, is a spy. Or, was a spy. A series of catastrophic incidents happened, and she finds herself decommissioned, in a room with a comatose person, and without any idea how she got here. There's a very dangerous game afoot in the fictional town of Portofiro, Zero Parades' setting, and your job is figuring it out and possibly even finding redemption. Maybe. If you can manage it.

Like its spiritual predecessor Disco Elysium, Zero Parades has standard CRPG elements like persuasion and knowledge, but unlike standard CRPGs, you're doing a lot more with them other than picking locks and lying to folks. With higher points in certain social or mental skills, you have a better chance of passing certain checks in conversations that unlock entirely new perspectives on what's happening. Sometimes, you just get a bit of extra lore. That's usually like the consolation prize in video games, but Zero Parades' impeccable writing means these moments are just as rewarding as stumbling onto a new story path.

On other occasions, you fall down a rabbit hole of madness and form a bond with a drunken businessman over your shared delusions about the idea of a goddess trampling you underfoot (for example). Which sounds fun, and it is, until your delusion stat maxes out and you die. The same can happen with fatigue and anxiety stats. Just like real life!

Balancing your more extreme decisions with less tumultuous ones is a big part of Zero Parades, but whatever choice you make, it always takes a "yes, and" approach. Even when what you've done seems very wrong, possibly even fatal, you nearly always have a way forward. It might just be very, very different from the path you thought you'd take. It keeps you in a state of perpetual uncertainty, like you have no idea what the right thing to do is and just have to wing it and hope for the best. In other words, you're thinking and behaving just like Hershel. I can't think of any other game that uses choices to let you embody a character on such an important level — not even the (also excellent) Disco Elysium.
2 Slay the Princess
Release date: Oct. 23, 2023
Where to play: PS4, PS5, Switch, Windows PC, Xbox One, Xbox Series X

The duo at Black Tabby love pushing the boundaries of choice-driven narratives, so in the middle of making the massive Scarlet Hollow, they set out to do something more contained and experimental with Slay the Princess. You're a valiant warrior, tasked with entering a cabin, descending to its basement, and slaying the princess imprisoned there. She is, the narrator assures you, quite dangerous. Not human at all, but a fiendish monster adopting the guise of an innocent maiden. What you do from here ripples out across the rest of the game in wildly unforeseen ways. Even refusing to enter the cabin is a valid choice, one that unlocks a whole new branch of the story.

When folks talk about games where choices matter, the conversation typically heads in one direction: how many endings there are. It's the logical endpoint of wondering how your choices will or won't matter. However, it overlooks other, equally important ways stories change based on how you interact with them. Slay the Princess embodies the best of both philosophies. The many and varied branches eventually resolve into a fixed set of potential endings, but the outcome is only half the story, or not even half, really. Each path — even the ones that share the same outcome — unfolds around some new facet of the situation, or yourself, or the princess, or a combination of all those things.

You make your choices guided solely by your instincts and what you're encouraged to believe based on other interactions. (E.g., if the princess murders you brutally in one run, you're a lot less likely to believe her protestations of innocence the next time.) It gives these branches an intensity that's unique to Slay the Princess and utterly impossible to have in a story where you're just wondering who lives or dies based on what you do.

Scarlet Hollow, Black Tabby's horror VN-slash-RPG-lite, is also very much worth your attention. It's technically not finished yet, even after five very substantial chapters, which is the only reason it's not on this list. But if you like good writing, unusual horror, good writing, top-notch art, a fresh take on romance, and good writing, you absolutely need to play it.
1 The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy
Release date: April 24, 2025
Where to play: Switch, Windows PC

You don't even make that many choices in The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy, but the ones you do make explode the game. Sometimes almost literally. The gist of it is that a group of kids get whisked away to a weird school after cuddly-looking murder monsters invade Tokyo. A strange ghost guy saved them and is now their headmaster-slash-military commander, and instead of lessons, they get blood magic that grants them superpowers so they can fight the monsters. That's just in the first 30 minutes.

For 30 hours, it forces you down a linear path with no branches, and the game ostensibly ends. Then it's back to the start, only this time, you can change how events unfold. It introduces this feature in a very dramatic way that signals just how big your choices are now: A single action transforms the entire storyline and the lives and trajectories of everyone in the school. Not always for the best, either.

It's like developer Too Kyoo took expectations about choice-driven games and decided to push them to their most extreme conclusions in every way imaginable. Last Defense Academy has 100 endings, and none of them are "canon." The absurd joke endings — there's a whole tree of story paths considered the "humor" path — are just as valid as the more serious and traumatic ones, even if they occasionally outstay their welcome. Who lives, who dies, and whether the ending is happy or sad all become moot points, replaced by variations of "what the hell could possibly happen next?" You're making the choices, but you have absolutely no control over what they lead to.

Imbuing a single choice with that much power and influence while taking most of the control from the player is just such an unexpected, even radical, thing to do in interactive media. It almost bankrupted Too Kyoo, so projects of that scale probably aren't the wisest ideas. But the way it defies expectation and turns the established relationship between the game and the player on its head is just superb and a big reason why it was one of our favorite games last year.

articles.headline: How to stop audio from auto-playing on Android Auto
keyFacts: Drivers can stop Android Auto from automatically playing audio by turning off the Start music automatically toggle in the device settings.
Spotify users report that the app still auto-plays even after changing settings because Bluetooth devices and accessories can send playback commands.
Solutions vary by vehicle and phone, requiring drivers to test different fixes such as unpairing Bluetooth or removing Spotify from Android Auto entirely.
body: How to stop audio from auto-playing on Android Auto
Because you probably don't want your stereo on at full blast the moment you start your car.

If you've ever started your car only to be blasted by music you didn't ask for, you already know the headache of Android Auto's autoplay quirk. The moment your phone connects, by USB or wirelessly (even if you use an adapter), your last playlist, podcast or audiobook picks up where it left off at whatever volume you had set the last time you were in the car. It's an unwelcome surprise during a morning commute and a real distraction if you prefer a few quiet seconds before pulling out of the driveway. Depending on what music or audiobooks you were listening to, it may also not be content you want the kids to hear when you're driving them to school.

In the past, fixing this problem was quite difficult and required a ton of workarounds, extra apps and jumping through hoops you really shouldn't have to. Now, it often just requires flipping a toggle.
How do I stop audio from auto-playing on Android Auto?

You'll need to start with Android Auto's own settings. You'll need to go to Settings > Connected devices > Android Auto and look under the Startup section. That's where you'll find the toggle for the Start music automatically feature. If you have trouble finding it, try searching for Android Auto in your settings. Switching this feature off tells Android Auto not to resume playback the moment it connects to your car. For loads of drivers, this single step solves the problem, and it's the first fix mentioned on Spotify's support forums.

If the toggle doesn't help, the issue may be happening at the Bluetooth level rather than inside Android Auto. Android Auto uses Bluetooth to route phone calls and to create the initial handshake between phone and car. One workaround to test is removing your phone from the car's Bluetooth memory and reconnecting with USB only, if your setup allows it. In some vehicles, that can reduce unwanted playback triggers, though results vary by car, phone and connection type.
Why does Spotify keep auto-playing in my car?

If you've already disabled Start music automatically and Spotify still starts on its own, you're not imagining things. Spotify users have reported this exact issue across community forums for years, with threads dating back to 2022 that remain active today. But it's worth noting that sometimes your car may not even be to blame at all. Any Bluetooth device paired with your phone, like headphones and speakers, can affect autoplay. According to Spotify's support team, the behavior depends on how a given Bluetooth device interacts with Spotify's API.

That distinction matters because Spotify cannot always prevent a connected device from sending a "play" command when it reconnects, powers on or resumes a media session. Before blaming your phone or reinstalling the app, check whether autoplay happens only with one Bluetooth device and test it with another speaker, headset or vehicle if possible. Keeping Spotify, your phone's operating system and the device firmware updated may reduce connection glitches, but there is no guaranteed universal fix when the command originates from the Bluetooth accessory.

Since Spotify prioritizes easy connections across thousands of hardware combinations, a universal fix isn't guaranteed anytime soon. Some drivers find success through Android Auto's settings, others through Spotify's app permissions and plenty report that neither option works consistently for their specific car or phone. If nothing pans out, you could just remove Spotify from Android Auto entirely, but that means that you won't be able to access Spotify from your car's display.

The bottom line is that you should start with Android Auto's Start music automatically toggle since it resolves the issue for many drivers. If music still plays uninvited, try the Bluetooth unpairing trick before removing the app from Android Auto entirely. Given how inconsistently Bluetooth behaves across car models, expect some trial and error.

articles.headline: Moonlighter studio won't host a public playtest of its next game due to rampant AI-led cloning: 'We know we're not the only developers feeling this way'
keyFacts: Digital Sun Games canceled a public playtest for its upcoming roguelike ReVamp due to fears of AI-driven cloning and reverse-engineering.
Marketing manager Israel Mallén stated that sharing a game build months before its March 2027 release feels too risky.
Other developers have also canceled public demos recently amid concerns that AI tools are enabling rapid duplication of unreleased games.
body: The studio behind the Moonlighter series has announced it will no longer host a public playtest for its forthcoming roguelike due to fears it will be "reverse-engineered, cloned and published". The move comes as a surge in rapidly vibe coded clones floods Steam, Roblox and mobile app stores in the aftermath of Claude Opus 5.5.

"With launch still months away, sharing a build with tens of thousands of players feels like too big a risk," Digital Sun Games' marketing manager Israel Mallén told PC Gamer. The game under discussion is ReVamp, a "tower defensevania" roguelike due for release in March 2027.
"We know we're not the only developers feeling this way, and the more this is talked about, the more likely platforms are to step in."

In its public announcement Digital Sun Games was fairly blunt. "We've been concerned by recent news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out. With launch still months away, a large public build of ReVamp felt like too big a risk."

Last week the studio behind Drunken Goddess Reflux canceled plans to roll out a public demo for Steam Next Fest due to similar fears. "We're concerned the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before launch," a spokesperson for the studio wrote.

Opus 5.5 has proven hugely disruptive to the games industry. It has aided several high profile game decompiles, helped jailbreak the PS5, led Xbox to announce its own AI-centric Xbox Labs, and made developing quickfire clones extremely easy. It's likely why this month's Steam Next Fest has over 8,000 demos, up from around 4,000 in June.

As I wrote yesterday, the speed at which clones can now be turned around is mind-boggling, and will have (is already having) huge ramifications for indie game development and marketing. When the creator of incremental punching game Escape the Walls published footage of their game on X, it was only ten days before at least seven clones were available on Roblox, and at least one on Steam.

Shaun Prescott is the Australian editor of PC Gamer. With over ten years experience covering the games industry, his work has appeared on GamesRadar+, TechRadar, The Guardian, PLAY Magazine, the Sydney Morning Herald, and more. Specific interests include indie games, obscure Metroidvanias, speedrunning, experimental games and FPSs. articles.headline: England coach should be English, suggests Fleming
keyFacts: England men's Test coach Stephen Fleming suggested that the national team should primarily be led by someone from England.
Fleming stated that developing English coaches is a priority of his tenure, supported by a heavily homegrown backroom staff.
Fleming will take charge of his first series in South Africa in December after being appointed in July.
body: - Published
New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, has suggested the national team should be led by someone from England.
Fleming, who will take charge of his first series in South Africa in December, is the latest overseas coach to lead the England men's team.
Since 1999, only two Englishmen - Peter Moores (twice) and Chris Silverwood - have been in charge of the Test side, while Ashley Giles had a spell as white-ball coach.

In the same time period England have been led by two Zimbabweans, in Duncan Fletcher and Andy Flower, and Australian Trevor Bayliss - while Fleming has succeeded his fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum, who remains white-ball coach. Another Australian, Matthew Mott, also had time in charge of the white-ball team.
Fleming's backroom team, announced last week, is heavily weighted towards homegrown coaches.
Former England opener Marcus Trescothick, who was in interim charge of the Test team earlier this year, is joined by ex-England wicketkeeper James Foster and former spinner Richard Dawson.
Jonathan Trott, an Ashes winner with England, is about to begin a spell in charge of England Lions. Both Trott and Dawson were in the running for the Test job before Fleming was appointed.
Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former New Zealand captain Fleming said it will be a "priority" of his tenure to help develop English coaches.
"I do believe that primarily the national team should be coached by a national representative," said Fleming.
"I'm grateful for the opportunity, but there will be some development in terms of the coaching, and you can see by our staff."
As well as Fleming and McCullum filling the head coach roles for the men's national teams, England's selector, Marcus North, is Australian.

In September it was announced that another Australian, Leah Poulton, will become the managing director of England women. Between 2020 and 2023 England women's head coach was Lisa Keightley, the former Australia international.
In addition to developing the coaches on his own staff, Fleming said he will also occasionally invite county coaches and former England players into the set-up.
"There are some really key people who have come back into the system and I'm really pleased about that," he said.

"I look forward to working with them, but it is a real focus and it's an ambition as well that you will also get county coaches who will be introduced at certain times and you will get past players that will be asked to come back as well.
"It's really inclusive and a comfortable nature of using what's around, but also driving what should be driven within the county game and the English game."
One of the criticisms of McCullum's four-year spell in charge of the Test team was his lack of time spent around the county game.
In September, Fleming visited some counties and also spoke of his affection for the domestic game in England. The former batter had spells as a player with Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Middlesex.
He confirmed he will spend part of next summer watching county cricket in the build-up to the home Ashes series.
"Yep, I'll be around and I really enjoyed this year getting to catch up," said Fleming. "A lot of the guys I played with are now in positions either coaching or the head positions at counties.
"It was good to catch up with those guys and get a feel for where the county game is at. I really enjoyed it and it will be a key part to continuing developing players."

Fleming was appointed in July, though did not take charge for the series against Pakistan in August and September, meaning his first series at the helm will be the three matches in South Africa in December and January.
The squad for that series is due to be named in the first week of November.
England did not pick a specialist spinner in any of the three Tests against Pakistan, instead fielding four frontline seamers.
In South Africa's ongoing Test against Australia in Gqeberha, the tourists have omitted Nathan Lyon despite the off-spinner sitting sixth on the all-time list of Test wicket-takers with 573.

Last week, Shoaib Bashir was named as the only specialist red-ball spinner on England's list of fully centrally contracted players, while Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White were given development deals.
Following the tour of South Africa, spin will play a big role on the two-Test tour of Bangladesh in February.
Asked if Bashir's contract means he is England's number-one spinner, Fleming said the Derbyshire man represents "continuity".
"I acknowledge there's a raft of spinners just below that, that at times are putting their hand up," said Fleming.
"There is a raft of spinners there and are probably looking for an opportunity, and finding those conditions, it could be Bangladesh, where there could be two or three that will come along.
"The team could look quite different and that's the horses for courses example.
"But Bashir has got some experience and is still very young. There's an aspect of still looking and developing, and trying to find that right combination in the spin department."

articles.headline: A Star Wars Battlefront 3 Made By Bungie Would Probably Be Great But Also A Waste
keyFacts: Lucasfilm is reportedly searching for a development partner to create Star Wars Battlefront 3, according to a rumor discussed by Jeff Grubb.
The rumor indicates that Bungie is one of the studios being considered for the project, alongside Electronic Arts DICE.
It remains uncertain who will ultimately develop the game or when a potential follow-up might be officially revealed.
body: It’s been almost a decade since Star Wars Battlefront 2 and fans have been eager for a follow-up. According to Giant Bomb cohost Jeff Grubb, Lucasfilm is indeed shopping around a Star Wars Battlefront 3, but it remains to be seen who might actually make it. According to the rumor, Bungie is one of the studios in the running.

The origins of this rumor are gnarly, so buckle up. Electronic Gaming Monthly recently released a compendium retrospective, and one of the bonuses as part of the Kickstarter was a new digital issue. That new issue reportedly featured the return of the Quartermann gossip column. That column contained a rumor that Lucasfilm wants to do a new Battlefront game.
Grubb featured the column on his Game Mess Morning podcast for October 19:

The suits at Lucasfilm have been aggressively deploying probe droids for a development partner to take on the task of creating a follow-up. So far, no one has fully stepped up, but yours truly is hearing two major game studios are circling the project like a couple of snowspeeders led by the completely unsurprising EA DICE who we can hope learned from their loot box lesson. If the Force is not entrusted to DICE, it could land at none other than Halo, Destiny, and Marathon developer Bungie.

There are now others claiming to have heard similar rumors, at least the part about Disney wanting a new Battlefront game. It’s a perfect moment for this rumor to flare up and get people talking. With Galactic Racer and Zero Company, Star Wars games are hot this fall. Bungie is in-between projects, with Marathon seemingly destined to wind down and Destiny 2 on pause outside of brining older content back to the game. Sony has been fine fielding licensed Marvel projects with Insomniac Games. Why not partner with Disney on Star Wars, too?

On the other hand, if there were to be a Battlefront 3, it seems obvious to have EA DICE return to the franchise, having already been successful at it twice, rather than embark on a completely new journey with a completely new studio. I also personally think it would be a waste to have Bungie toil away for years adding to the Star Wars toybox when it’s already given us two of the best sci-fi franchises in gaming of the last decade plus when it comes to world building with both Destiny and Marathon. All things being equal, I’d rather see Bungie make another newÂ IP.

All things aren’t equal, however. Bungie is a shell of the studio that made those earlier games and it needs a win. Sony, I’m sure, would like to see the Bellevue-based office start generating real revenue again, even if it’s on another company’s terms. Battlefront 3 is more of a slam dunk than years of prototyping and pre-production on something completely new with a Bungie that’s been completely fractured since it was acquired.

One way or another, it would still be nice to get another Battlefront one of these days. Given how long it takes to ship AAA games these days, we’ll probably be deep into the PlayStation 6/Xbox Project Helix console cycle before one even gets revealed.

articles.headline: While You Wait For The Phasmophobia Movie, Don’t Miss This Hidden Gem
keyFacts: The horror film Never After Dark follows a young ghost-communicating intermediary named Airi on a difficult assignment.
The movie shares notable similarities with the game Phasmophobia and is described as a J-Horror revival project.
Never After Dark is currently playing in limited US theaters and will have its rent-at-home premiere on October 28.
body: An official Phasmophobia movie is on the way; we learned as much last summer . But what if I said you could watch something quite like Kinetic's ghostbusting co-op game right now?

That's the elevator pitch I bring you, fellow horror fans, less than two weeks out from Halloween. The movie is Never After Dark, a gorgeously shot, cleverly creepy ghost story that Phasmophobia fans shouldn't miss.

Never After Dark tells the story of Airi, a young woman who can commune with ghosts. She works as a traveling intermediary between the dead and the living, convincing spirits to move on and freeing residents from their hauntings. But on her latest gig, she discovers she's taken on a much harder assignment. And wow, that assignment looked really familiar in such a fun way.

Never After Dark has been described as a "J-Horror revival" project, recalling the ghost stories frequently imported to the US from Japan at the turn of the 21st Century. Movies like Ringu, Pulse, Dark Water, and Ju-On: The Grudge were a big deal in Japan and earned a lot of praise (and remakes, for better or worse) here in the States, too. I've never been a big fan of the term J-Horror, but I can see how it works as shorthand for that particular bundle of films.
Sorry, Airi, but there's no option to stay in the van and watch the cameras.

Director Dave Boyle is an American, but he has spent much of his career making movies in and about Japan. Some of those aforementioned inspirations for Never After Dark are my favorites in the genre, and Boyle's new film does indeed feel like them at times, though I was more often struck by how much it felt like I was playing a round of Phasmophobia. Even Airi, who works alone most of the time, finds herself with a small group of other characters, like a solo player hopping into an open lobby in Phasmophobia. I won't spoil the movie, but suffice it to say that many of the game's core mechanics and moments are reflected in it. Some scenes even feel pulled straight from the game.

Of course, this is partly because both Kinetic's game and Boyle's film draw on real-life theories about ghosts and how to interact with them, rather than the movie intentionally cribbing the game's core identity. Still, it made me wonder how the eventual Phasmophobia movie might handle some similar situations.

Never After Dark is in theaters across the US right now, albeit in limited release, so check that it's playing near you. Alternatively, you could also stream it at home soon. I haven't seen any announcement about whether it'll end up on any subscription service, but its rent-at-home premiere is set for October 28, making it a smart choice for Halloween weekend if you feel like you've seen everything scary and need something new.

I went into the movie because I'd heard about its nearly perfect aggregate review score and because I thought it might feel like something from my favorite director, Kiyoshi Kurosawa. It definitely checked that box, I'm happy to say, but just as central to its vibe is a fascinating look at what a Phasmophobia movie might look like--before we get the real thing in the (hopefully near) future.
