articles.headline: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
keyFacts: Pennsylvania health officials issued an alert Monday regarding rising cases of measles in pregnancy and congenital measles.
State health data shows 1,286 measles cases, 247 hospitalizations, and six reported deaths across 42 counties as of October 19.
Unvaccinated pregnant individuals face severe health risks from measles, while the MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy.
body: Pennsylvania’s health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn’t been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory.

The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania.

As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally).

The Pennsylvania health department did not immediately respond to a request for information from Ars Technica. But reporting from The 19th earlier this month put the number of measles cases during pregnancy at 53. At least one case of congenital measles led to a death; the first death reported in the current outbreak was in a newborn baby boy, who died immediately after birth while his mother was severely ill with measles.
Risky infection

Pregnant people who have not been vaccinated against measles nor previously had the infection are susceptible. A case of measles during pregnancy increases the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, the need for oxygen support or mechanical ventilation, and death. It also increases the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and preterm labor. The MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine and poses a theoretical risk of causing an infection in a fetus. If a pregnant person is exposed to the virus, they’re recommended to receive intravenous immunoglobulin to help protect against infection—but only if it is given within six days of exposure.

articles.headline: Why the Trump administration is fighting over a golf course
keyFacts: Donald Trump announced that Washington, DC's East Potomac Golf Links will close next month to become a single professional-caliber course.
A preservation group previously sued over the plan, which would eliminate a popular public park and historic cherry trees.
Trump stated his administration has an absolute right to renovate without approval, setting up a larger clash with federal courts.
body: A golfer plays on the course at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, DC, on October 19, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to take over a public park.

What’s happening? On Sunday, Trump announced in a social media post that East Potomac Golf Links, a municipal golf course on the Potomac River in Washington, DC, would close next month for what he described as “restoration work” to transform it from a three-course complex into a single professional-caliber course.

According to a rendering of the “restoration” shared by Trump, the new course would also eliminate a popular public park and multiuse road around the course, which is currently home to some of DC’s historic cherry trees.
Why does this matter? Relative to many other Trump decisions (like, say, the Iran war or interfering with Ukraine’s ability to defend itself), the fate of a golf course is not so high-stakes.

But it’s shaping up to be a major legal fight over the administration’s blitzkrieg approach to Washington that saw the East Wing of the White House demolished last year and Trump’s name attached to (and subsequently removed from) the Kennedy Center.

A DC preservation group previously sued over Trump’s plan to transform the course, which has been in the works for months prior to Sunday’s announcement. And the administration was already in hot water with a DC District Court judge over the recent removal of more than 500 trees from the course, which it described at the time as maintenance rather than part of Trump’s renovation scheme.
Trump, for his part, has said that his administration has “an absolute right” to renovate the course and does not need approval, setting him on a course for a bigger clash with federal courts.

What’s the big picture? Setting aside everything else about Trump’s golf course push, it’s unlikely — with just 15 days until the midterms — that this is a fight that will endear him or his party to voters, who are broadly fed up with corruption, inflation, and the overall cost of living.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Hi readers, happy Monday! Early voting is getting underway in some states and while The Logoff officially encourages you not to read too much — or anything, really — into early voting numbers, I do recommend this post from the Substack newsletter Can We Still Govern? by Don Moynihan. He rounded up some of the best “I voted” stickers with art submitted by (mostly) children, ranging from charming to deeply strange. You can find them all here .
As always, thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

articles.headline: Alberta voters decide whether to take a step toward separating from Canada
keyFacts: Alberta voters are deciding whether to take the first step toward a referendum on separating from Canada.
A government-commissioned report estimates that separating from Canada could cost Alberta up to 170 billion Canadian dollars over five years.
Elections Alberta expects unofficial results from the vote within 48 hours after polls close.
body: Alberta voters decide whether to take a step toward separating from Canada
In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Voters in Alberta, Canada, are deciding today whether to take the first step toward a referendum on separating from the rest of the country. Reporter Sheena Rossiter joins us from Edmonton, which is the capital of Alberta. Hi there.
SHEENA ROSSITER, BYLINE: Hello.
SUMMERS: So, Sheena, this vote's a nonbinding referendum. Explain for us a bit more what people in Alberta are voting on today.

ROSSITER: Well, essentially, it's a vote on whether to have another referendum. There are 10 questions covering everything from immigration and provincial services to Alberta's constitutional status. Question 10 is the key one. Voters choose between keeping Alberta in Canada or starting the process towards a separation referendum. If Option 2 wins, it could pave the way for a vote on separation, much like Brexit in the U.K.
SUMMERS: And these separatist sentiments there, how long have they been brewing in Alberta?

ROSSITER: These grievances go back decades. Some people I spoke with at the Alberta independence rally have been separatists for 25 years, like Cory Morgan. He is the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group advocating for an independent Alberta.
CORY MORGAN: Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand something large is brewing here. And if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow.

ROSSITER: Separatist sentiment really grew during COVID, with frustration spilling onto the streets during the 2022 trucker convoy in Ottawa. Now, the premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, called for a referendum but wants Alberta to stay in Canada. And Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, is making the same case, saying, quote, "Canada is stronger together."
SUMMERS: What's really at the heart of this, though?

ROSSITER: Well, Alberta is a major oil-producing province. It's the wealthiest province in the Canadian Confederation, and some residents feel that they contribute more to Canada than they get back. They want to keep more of that money in Alberta. But a government-commissioned report from the University of Calgary estimates that Alberta separating from Canada could cost up to $170 billion Canadian over five years. Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity group campaigning against Alberta separation, points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic fallout.
THOMAS LUKASZUK: Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces. And till today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that.
SUMMERS: How soon will we know the results?

ROSSITER: Well, Elections Alberta says unofficial results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing. There's also a legal challenge over Indigenous rights, with the province appealing a court ruling that First Nations weren't properly consulted. And whatever the result, Alberta's place in Canada is likely to remain a major issue heading into next year's provincial election.
SUMMERS: Sheena Rossiter, reporting from Edmonton, Alberta, thanks much.
ROSSITER: Thank you.

articles.headline: Arsenal and Liverpool backed to take advantage of Barcelona’s mad decision to sell best defender
keyFacts: European football journalist Andy Brassell stated that Barcelona may sell defender Jules Kounde in the near future.
Brassell said that Premier League clubs Arsenal and Liverpool are potential destinations for the 27-year-old player.
Brassell warned that offloading Kounde would be a mad decision for the Spanish club.
body: France defender Jules Kounde has been tipped to move to the Premier League if Barcelona choose to cash in on him.
The LaLiga giants have been warned it would be a ‘mad’ decision to offload Kounde anytime soon, though.
Kounde has been with Barcelona since 2022 Getty
That is according to European football journalist Andy Brassell, who has named the two Premier League clubs the right-back could join.
Kounde has made 196 appearances for Barca since signing from Sevilla in 2022.
He has also won three LaLiga titles in four years, with another potentially on the cards this term.
Hansi Flick’s side are already five points clear at the top of the table having won each of their opening nine matches.
Kounde has helped contribute with a goal and an assist in their last two victories.
However, Brassell believes Barca may chose to sell the 27-year-old sooner rather than later despite handing him a new five-year deal as recently as August last year.
Could Kounde leave Barcelona?
Speaking exclusively to talkSPORT.com, he explained: “I do get the feeling that Barcelona are going to sell Jules Kounde at some point in the near future, which I think is a bit mad.
“Obviously they’re going to have to sell someone of value at some point in the medium term. It looks like they’re limbering up for it to be him.
“He’s an underrated right-back and a really underrated centre-back because he doesn’t get to play there that often anymore.”
Kounde has shown his versatility for club and country at both right-back and in central defence.
Barca have been warned selling Kounde would be a ‘mad’ decision Getty
As well as his title triumphs with Barcelona, the former Sevilla and Bordeaux man has won 58 caps for France.
He was part of the side which reached the 2022 World Cup final having won the Nations League the previous year.
Kounde made five starts during the tournament in Qatar, including the final defeat to Argentina.
Didier Deschamps later included him in his squad for both Euro 2024 and last summer’s World Cup in North America.
Arsenal and Liverpool told to sign Kounde
As for which clubs Brassell believes Kounde could join, he continued: “I think he’d be brilliant for Arsenal , for example. I think he’d be really good there.
“You could argue that maybe that’s the place that Arsenal don’t need to spend £50-60million on a player because they’ve got so many accomplished defenders.
Kounde was handed a new five-year deal by Barca last summer AFP
“I think he’d be good for Liverpool as well because he can be an attacking full-back but he’s an authentic defender as well.”
Arsenal currently have just two senior right-backs in their squad in the form of Jurrien Timber and Ben White .
However, the latter is currently out of contract at the end of next season.
As for Liverpool, the Reds’ centre-back options could see them move for Kounde next summer.
Both Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez’s deal will expire at the end of the current campaign.
Their exits would leave Andoni Iraola with only three recognised centre-backs, provided Ronald Araujo’s loan from Barca is made permanent.
Arsenal have an embarrassment of riches in defence but Arteta surely wouldn’t say no to Kounde Getty
Van Dijk’s potential departure from Liverpool in the summer leaves a hole in their defence Getty
Kounde’s ability to play both centrally and at right-back would also provide a boost, with Araujo deputising in the role in recent weeks.
It comes amid Conor Bradley’s injury lay-off , with a return not expected before December for the long-term absentee.

articles.headline: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, says court filing
keyFacts: US prosecutors stated in a court filing that former OpenAI worker Abdulrahman Alfozan received significant support from the Saudi government after allegedly planting a recording device.
Alfozan was denied bail by a US district judge on Monday after being deemed a flight risk following his arrest by the FBI on October 9.
The FBI investigation remains ongoing, and Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a fine if convicted.
body: - Published

A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan was scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

articles.headline: Moonlighter dev delays Steam playtest for its "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp over concerns that AI copycats might clone it before launch
keyFacts: Developer Digital Sun delayed the Steam playtest for its game ReVamp due to concerns about AI-powered cloning.
The studio will now host a smaller, contained playtest on Discord starting October 29th to mitigate risks.
Digital Sun plans to open a public playtest for ReVamp around January before the game's full launch in March 2027.
body: Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out."

The developer was planning to let folks into its vampiric "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp near the end of this spooky month, but a new trend of gen-AI copycats cloning both old and unreleased games left the studio worried.

"So many of you signed up for ReVamp's first playtest here on Steam (thank you!), but we've decided to start with something more contained on our Discord, with the public playtest coming a bit later," the developer wrote in a recent Steam blog post.

Digital Sun pointed the finger at "news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out," and worried that "sharing a build with tens of thousands of players" months prior to its full launch is "too big a risk."

From here, Digital Sun will grant access to ReVamp's first playtest in waves starting from the 29th of October, via Discord. "Even if you don't get in right away, we'd love for you to join the conversation around ReVamp as we let more players in. We hope to open the public playtest around January. To everyone who requested access here on Steam: we're sorry for the change of plans, and thank you for your patience," the studio added.
ReVamp launches in full on 25th March, 2027. Here's hoping the move can successfully shoo away any would-be clones.
Digital Sun isn't the only developer having to work around the gen-AI boom. Xbox recently announced an entire department that sounds like it's focused on gen-AI game-making, as just one example.

Meanwhile, Alliance Arts outright cancelled a Steam Next Fest demo for its anime-inspired Russian Roulette game, Drunken Goddess Reflux, because of similar issues. "We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the company said last week.

Steam Next Fest 2026 should be a great occasion to discover new and exciting games that were previously nowhere near your radar. However, as we reported earlier today, the shadow of generative AI looms over the entire event and could dampen an otherwise great Steam tradition.
